notes.subject: plate
notes.text: Plates use red characters, recognisable even through the blur.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: White bollards with a rectangular yellow reflector on the front and white on the back; a dark brown type has two red stripes at the top.

notes.subject: guardrail
notes.text: A-type guardrails carry yellow reflectors, shared in Europe only with Spain and Andorra.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Mostly square concrete poles with tiny holes and small metal wrappings; the second most common type has oval holes.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Pedestrian signs have two horizontal dotted lines, no zebra stripes, and a square-headed figure.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Road signs often have an extra small blue plate where other countries use a white one.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Signposts are often orange, and so are the backs of signs, which is unique here.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Priority signs have an orange diamond and are much smaller than elsewhere.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: White chevrons with a red arrow; they are not used in the neighbour to the south.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Kilometre markers are often green, sometimes with red text.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Town entry signs are white with a black border and bold black text.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Red hydrant signs with an H on top.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Bus stops are marked with yellow signposts, and shelters often have yellow roofs.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Street name signs vary by city, are short and tall, and often show the municipality; the northern neighbour's are long and wide.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: All lines are white and roads often have bike lanes on both sides; bike paths have short dashed outer lines.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Many rural roads are made of concrete slabs, which the northern neighbour almost never uses.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Almost every road, big or small, has gutters on both sides.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Houses of distinctive red brick are common in the north and west; southern houses use grey stone and look more like the southern neighbour's.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Flat in the northwest, especially near the coast, getting hillier toward the southeast.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Lots of blurred houses, second only to its eastern neighbour; a red car with a long antenna appears rarely.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: Three languages: a northern tongue (z, w, ee, ij), a southern Romance one (ç, é, è, à) and a small eastern pocket with ä, ü, ö, ß; the capital is bilingual.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Bus stop signs have a white top in the north and the capital, and a yellow top in the south.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: In the north and capital, most warning signs have a thick red outline with no white border; the south usually has a thin white one.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Traffic lights on yellow-and-black poles are unique to the north; the south and capital often use red-and-white.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Landlines have 9 digits; the 1 or 2 digits after the leading 0 give the area code. Mobiles start with 04 and have 10 digits.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: The Ardennes in the southeast have steep hills, dense forest and valleys.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Very flat polders below sea level with many waterways lie near the coast and the northern border, often confused with the northern neighbour.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Much of the coast is lined with apartment blocks, mockingly called a wall; dunes with low bushes and long grass also appear.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: A northeastern town of tangled enclaves marks borders with small white crosses; street signs show which country you are in.
